title: Convergence tests
examples: When should I use the ratio test instead of the comparison test?
How do I find the radius of convergence for a power series?
What is the main difference between the comparison test and the limit comparison test?

explain.say: Today we learn about tests for series convergence. We check if a series adds up to a finite number. We look at the ratio test first. This test uses the ratio of terms. For example, check the series one over n factorial. You calculate the ratio of the next term to the current term. If the limit is less than one, the series converges.

items: Calculate ratio of next term to current

explain.say: Next we use the comparison test. We compare our series to a known series. We need to know if the larger series converges or diverges. For example, compare one over n squared to a p-series. Since p is two, the larger series converges. Therefore, our series also converges.

draw.text: Comparison Test: Compare to known series

explain.say: The alternating series test is for alternating signs. The terms must alternate between positive and negative. For example, consider one over n multiplied by negative one. We check if the magnitude decreases to zero. If it does, the series converges.

draw.text: Alternating Series Test: Terms decrease to zero

explain.say: We can find the radius of convergence for power series. We use the ratio test on the coefficients. If the limit is one over R, then R is the radius. For example, for x over n, the radius is one. This means it converges for x between negative one and one.

items: R is the radius of convergence

faq.q: When should I use the ratio test?
faq.a: Use the ratio test when the terms involve factorials or exponents. It is very effective for those types of terms. You can also use it when finding the radius of convergence.
asks: What is the best test for factorials?
When is the ratio test most useful?

faq.q: What is the difference between the comparison test and the limit comparison test?
faq.a: The comparison test requires you to show one series is smaller than another. The limit comparison test is often easier; you just take the limit of the ratio of the terms. If that limit is a positive number, both series behave the same way.
asks: How do I choose between the two comparison tests?

faq.q: Does the alternating series test always work?
faq.a: No, the test only applies if the terms are alternating in sign. You must check two things: the terms must decrease in magnitude, and the limit of the terms must be zero. If either fails, the test does not apply.
asks: What if the terms do not decrease?
What if the signs are not alternating?

faq.q: What does the radius of convergence tell me?
faq.a: It tells you the interval around zero where the power series is guaranteed to converge. The series converges for values of x within a distance R from zero. It does not tell you about convergence exactly at the endpoints.
asks: What is the interval of convergence?
Does R tell me everything about convergence?

faq.q: Can I use the ratio test on any series?
faq.a: You can always try the ratio test, but it might not give a clear answer. If the limit is exactly one, the test is inconclusive, and you must use another test. Always check the other tests if L equals one.
asks: What if the limit is one?
Is the ratio test always conclusive?

facts: The ratio test is useful when terms involve factorials or powers of n.
The comparison test requires comparing a series to a known convergent or divergent series.
The alternating series test requires the terms' magnitudes to decrease to zero.
For a power series, the radius of convergence R is found using the ratio test.
If the limit from the ratio test is less than one, the series converges absolutely.

quiz.say: Determine convergence for the series one over n squared.

options.show: Converges only if n is even
options.say: Converges only if n is even

quiz.why: This is a p-series with p equal to two. Since two is greater than one, the series converges by the p-series test.

wrong.0: The series must be summed over all positive integers, not just even ones.
wrong.2: This is a common mistake because students confuse it with the harmonic series, which has p equal to one.
wrong.3: The ratio test is overkill here; the p-series test is direct and simpler.

quiz.say: Find the radius of convergence for the series x over n.
quiz.why: Using the ratio test limit gives one over one, so the radius of convergence R is one.

wrong.1: This suggests the series only converges at x equals zero, which is incorrect here.
wrong.2: This would mean the series converges for all real numbers, which is not true for this series.
wrong.3: The radius must be a single constant value, not dependent on n.

quiz.say: Determine convergence for the series (-1 / n) multiplied by one over n.

options.show: Diverges by the nth term test
options.say: Diverges by the nth term test

quiz.why: The terms alternate signs, and the magnitude one over n squared decreases to zero, so it converges.

wrong.0: The comparison test is unnecessary because the alternating series test is more direct here.
wrong.1: While the ratio test might be inconclusive, the alternating series test provides a definitive answer.
wrong.3: The terms go to zero, so the nth term test is passed, meaning it might converge.
